What goes into a roof,
specified properly.

A good quote says exactly what is going on your roof. Here is what each part is, the UK standard it should meet and why it matters, so you can compare any quote like for like.

Breathable underlay

The membrane laid over the rafters and under the battens. Most modern re-roofs use a vapour-permeable (breathable) underlay. Older roofs often have bitumen felt, such as Type 1F.

  • Laid from the eaves upwards, with the overlaps the manufacturer specifies
  • Supported at the eaves, so water runs into the gutter and not behind the fascia
  • Dressed over the valley boards, with the battens fixed through it to the rafters

Why it matters: It is the roof’s second line of defence. It catches wind-driven rain and lets moisture vapour escape from the loft, which helps prevent condensation and timber decay.

Tile battens

The timber strips fixed across the rafters that the tiles or slates hang from.

  • Graded, preservative-treated softwood to BS 5534
  • Commonly 25 × 38mm where rafters are no more than 450mm apart, and 25 × 50mm up to 600mm. Natural slate normally uses 25 × 50mm
  • Spaced at the gauge the tile manufacturer sets, which depends on the tile and its headlap. For one common concrete tile, for example, it is about 345mm at a 75mm headlap
  • Counter battens, commonly 25 × 50mm, are used in some builds and run up the slope over the rafters

Why it matters: The batten spacing decides how straight, how well lapped and how watertight the finished roof is. Cut batten ends at verges should be treated with preservative.

Tiles, headlap and fixings

Every tile has a minimum roof pitch and a minimum headlap (the overlap between one course and the next). Both come from the manufacturer’s data for that tile.

  • Minimum pitch varies by tile: for example around 30° to 35° for many clay plain tiles, and roughly 15° to 22.5° for many concrete interlocking tiles, with a few low-pitch designs going lower. A granular finish usually needs a steeper pitch than a smooth one
  • The lower the pitch, the bigger the headlap has to be
  • Tiles are fixed with corrosion-resistant nails and clips to a fixing schedule that follows BS 5534, with extra fixings at the edges where wind uplift is highest

Why it matters: The wrong tile for the roof pitch, or too few fixings, is a classic cause of leaks and slipped tiles in storms.

Ridge, hips and verges

The lines where roof slopes meet, and the edge of the roof at a gable end.

  • BS 5534 requires ridge and hip tiles to be mechanically fixed, not just bedded in mortar
  • Dry-fix systems tested to BS 8612:2018 clamp the tiles to ridge or hip battens, include ventilation and need no mortar maintenance
  • Dry verge systems fix the verge tiles mechanically, with an undercloak supporting the tile edge
  • Mortar-bedded ridges and hips are still used, particularly on older and listed buildings, but they should also be mechanically fixed. Bedded hips use a hip iron at the foot to stop the bottom tile slipping

Why it matters: The ridge, hips and verges take the worst of the wind and weather. Failed mortar and loose ridge tiles are a common reason for roof repairs.

Valleys: lead or GRP dry valley

A valley carries a lot of water, so it needs a proper lining. The two usual options are lead sheet and a GRP dry valley trough. A quote should say which one is being used.

Lead valley

  • Lead sheet to BS EN 12588, Code 5 or heavier, depending on length and exposure
  • Laid over valley boards and dressed over tilting fillets, with the tiles or slates cut back to leave an open channel
  • Detailed to Lead Sheet Association guidance

GRP dry valley

  • A glass-reinforced polyester (GRP) trough, typically 3m long and around 360mm wide, in grey UV-stabilised material
  • Mortar-free. Suits rafter pitches from 17.5° to 60°, with up to 20° difference between the two slopes
  • Fixed over valley boards that extend at least 50mm beyond its edges, with the outer welts nailed at 500mm maximum centres
  • Where it meets the ridge or another valley, a lead saddle (Code 4 minimum) is dressed over the joint

Why it matters: Either can be right. The choice depends on the two roof pitches, the covering and the look wanted, which is why a quote should state which is being used and, for lead, which code.

Everything above
your head, sorted.

From a few slipped tiles to a complete new roof, we find out what is actually wrong, explain it in plain English and give you a clear price.

Re-roofing and tiling

Cracked, slipping or moss-covered tiles can only be patched so many times. A re-roof strips the old covering back to the rafters, adds a new breathable membrane and battens, then lays new tiles or slate, with the ridge, hips and verges mechanically fixed to BS 5534, and the valleys and lead flashings detailed properly.

Flat roofing

Garages, extensions, porches and dormers: flat roofs usually fail at the joints, the edges and around rooflights. We fit felt and liquid-applied waterproofing with proper upstands, so rainwater runs away instead of pooling.

Fascias, soffits and guttering

Your roofline is how rainwater leaves the house. Fascias carry the gutters, soffits close the overhang and downpipes take the water to the drain. When they fail, water runs down your walls and causes damp.

Roof repairs

A leak doesn’t always mean a new roof. We trace where the water is really getting in, whether that’s a slipped tile, a worn flashing, a tired valley or the chimney, and fix that.

Property maintenance

Small jobs done early save big bills later. We look after homeowners and landlords with general upkeep, from loose ridge tiles and blocked gutters to the repairs that keep a property sound.

Repair it,
or replace it?

Not every leak needs a new roof, and not every old roof is worth patching. Here is how to tell the difference.

Usually a repair

  • A handful of slipped, cracked or missing tiles
  • One leak you can trace to a single spot, such as the chimney, a valley or a wall junction
  • Worn lead flashing, or cracked mortar around the ridge and hips
  • Gutters or fascias that are blocked, leaking or starting to rot

Usually a re-roof

  • Tiles crumbling, flaking or cracking across the whole roof
  • Leaks in several places, or damp patches that keep coming back
  • A sagging roof line, or rotten battens and rafters visible from the loft
  • Old underlay that is torn or brittle, with daylight showing through

An old roof often shows several of these at once. Not sure which applies to yours? Tell us what you are seeing and your postcode, and we will tell you honestly which it is when we quote.

Questions
people ask.

Do I need a new roof, or will a repair do?

Often a repair is enough: a few slipped tiles or one failed flashing. If the problem is widespread, such as crumbling tiles, repeated leaks or rotten timbers, a re-roof is usually better value than patching. The repair-or-replace guide above covers the common signs.

Where do most leaks come from?

Usually not the middle of the tiles. Water tends to get in at the joints: chimney flashings, valleys, ridge and hip tiles, wall junctions and roof windows.

What is the difference between a lead valley and a dry valley?

A lead valley is lead sheet (Code 5 or heavier) dressed over valley boards. A dry valley is a mortar-free GRP trough, typically 3m long, for rafter pitches from 17.5° to 60°. Both can be right. The spec guide above shows each, and your quote should say which is used.

Should ridge and hip tiles be dry-fixed or bedded in mortar?

Either way, BS 5534 requires them to be mechanically fixed. Dry-fix systems tested to BS 8612:2018 are now the norm because they hold the tiles securely, ventilate the roof and avoid cracking mortar. Mortar-bedded ridges are still used, particularly on older and listed buildings.

Will you need scaffolding?

For most re-roofs, and many repairs on two-storey homes, yes. It keeps the work safe and lets the job be done properly. We will explain what is needed, and what it adds to the price, when we quote.

How long will it take?

It depends on the size and shape of the roof, how much timber needs repairing and the weather. We will give you a realistic idea of timescale with your quote.

Do I need planning permission or Building Regulations approval?

In England and Wales, re-roofing is normally controlled by Building Regulations. As a guide, the Planning Portal says you will not normally need to submit an application if the work affects less than 50% of the roof (and under 25% of the building’s whole envelope). Re-roofing a larger area usually does, and roof insulation normally has to be upgraded where that is practical. A roofer registered with a competent person scheme can self-certify, otherwise it goes through Building Control. Listed buildings and conservation areas have extra rules, and Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own systems.

Can you work on flat roofs, garages and extensions?

Yes. Flat roofing is one of our services, including felt and liquid-applied systems and the details around rooflights and edges.

Roofing words,
in plain English.

Quotes make a lot more sense when you know the terms. Here is what the common ones mean, and why they matter.

Ridge

The line along the very top of the roof where two slopes meet. Ridge tiles cap it. BS 5534 requires ridge and hip tiles to be mechanically fixed, and dry-fix systems to BS 8612 are now the norm.

Hip

The sloping line where two roof slopes meet at an outward corner, running from the ridge down to the eaves. Bedded hips use a metal hip iron at the foot to stop the bottom tile slipping. Dry hips use support trays and clips.

Valley

The inward angle where two slopes meet. It carries a lot of water, so it is lined with lead sheet (Code 5 or heavier) or a GRP dry valley trough.

Dry valley

A mortar-free valley made from a glass-reinforced polyester (GRP) trough, typically 3m long and fixed over valley boards. It suits rafter pitches from 17.5° to 60°, with up to 20° difference between the two slopes.

Verge

The edge of the roof at a gable end. A dry verge system fixes the verge tiles mechanically instead of relying on mortar. An undercloak supports the tiles, and the board under the edge is the bargeboard.

Flashing

Waterproof strips, usually lead, that seal the joints where a roof meets a wall or chimney. Failed flashings are one of the most common causes of leaks.

Soaker

A small piece of lead dressed under each tile or slate and turned up the wall, used with stepped flashings where a roof meets a wall.

Lead code

The number that tells you how thick a sheet of lead is. Code 4 is 1.80mm, Code 5 is 2.24mm and Code 6 is 2.65mm. A quote should state which code is being used.

Eaves

The lower edge of the roof, where it overhangs the wall and carries the gutter.

Fascia and soffit

The fascia is the board along the eaves that the gutters fix to. The soffit is the panel under the overhang. Rot here is a sign water has been getting in.

Breathable membrane

The underlay under the battens. It catches wind-driven rain and lets moisture escape from the loft. Older roofs often have bitumen felt instead.

Battens and gauge

Battens are the timber strips the tiles hang from. The gauge is the distance between them, which is set by the tile and its headlap.

Headlap

The overlap between one course of tiles and the next. The minimum depends on the tile and the roof pitch, and comes from the manufacturer.

Rooflight

A window set into the roof, fitted on a kerb or upstand and flashed so water stays out.
